reproduction_number_range.source: Gani and Leach 2001, Nature, abstract via Europe PMC: 3.5 to 6 in isolated pre-twentieth century populations with negligible herd immunity; earlier estimates 1.5 to above 20 are disputed

transmissibility_per_day.source: Midpoint of the sourced reproduction number range (4.75) divided by the infectious days; not itself observed

case_fatality.source: CDC smallpox overview, stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/26503: about 30 percent overall in variola major (first-contact fatality is disputed and is not this number)

immunity.source: CDC clinical signs page (cdc.gov/smallpox/hcp/clinical-signs): 'Recovery from smallpox gives the patient prolonged immunity to re-infection with variola virus'; Vichniakov 1968, Bulletin of the WHO 39(3):433-437 (abstract opened, PMC2554405): most who recover have lifelong immunity to a second attack, but some lose it more or less quickly. Permanent is the majority case; the exceptions are not quantified in what was opened

stage.incubating.source: CDC smallpox overview: incubation averages about 12 to 14 days, range 7 to 17. Shape 8 is a derived Erlang approximation of a bell-shaped period

stage.infectious.source: CDC smallpox overview, stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/26503: 'Most scabs will have fallen off three weeks after the rash appears' and 'The person is contagious to others until all of the scabs have fallen off'; the 21 day mean is the rash-to-scab span (the 2 to 4 day prodrome, when only sometimes contagious, is not counted)

density_exponent.source: Wikipedia, Basic reproduction number (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_reproduction_number, opened): R0 = contact rate / recovery rate, the contact rate set by 'the number of susceptible people in the population that the infected people contact'; whether contact rises with density is not stated there. Chowell et al., 1918 influenza in England and Wales (PMC2596813, opened): 'we found no association between transmissibility, death rates and indicators of population density and residential crowding', R between 1.3 and 1.9, and deaths scaling as population to the power 0.71-0.77 in rural areas and about 1.0 in towns. So the exponent of contact on crowding lies between 0 (that study) and 1 (mass action, density-dependent contact); 0.5 is the midpoint, a ballpark. Rader et al. 2020 (Nature Medicine; search summary only, full text not opened): crowded cities have longer epidemics and larger attack rates.
